cards.explanation: The answer is that they want to know who gave Him His authority, friends. The chief priests and elders come up to Him in the temple courts and ask, “By what authority are You doing these things?” Then they add, “And who gave You this authority?” They want to know where His authority for doing these things comes from.

The answer is True, friends. Jesus says, “I will also ask you one question…” and then, “…if you answer Me, I will tell you by what authority I am doing these things.” One question, one answer, and they get theirs. Sounds like the easiest trade in the temple courts.

The word is heaven, friends. Jesus asks, “What was the source of John’s baptism? Was it from heaven or from men?” John is the one who baptized people, and Jesus wants to know where that baptism came from. It's a short question with two choices, and neither one is comfortable for the leaders.

The follow-up question is, why then did they not believe him, friends. The leaders say, “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ He will ask, ‘Why then did you not believe him?’” If John's baptism came from heaven, then not believing John looks like a problem. They can already hear the follow-up before they've even answered the first question.

The answer is the people, friends. The leaders say, “But if we say, ‘From men,’ we are afraid of the people, for they all regard John as a prophet.” So the crowd is the problem with that answer. These leaders came to ask the questions, and now they're counting heads.

The answer is “We do not know,” friends. After they deliberated among themselves, the text says they answered, “We do not know.” Think about that for a second. They huddled up, and the final answer was four words long. I've burned a whole batch with less effort than that.

The answer is False, friends. Jesus had said He'd tell them if they answered His question. When they say, “We do not know.” He replies, “Neither will I tell you by what authority I am doing these things.” No answer from them, no answer from Him.

The answer is that he changes his mind and goes, friends. The first son said, “I will not…” but then the text says, “…later he changed his mind and went.” The no didn't have the last word. He ended up in the vineyard anyway.
The second son says, “I will, sir…” friends. Polite, quick and agreeable. Sounds great, doesn't it? Hold on to that answer, because Jesus is about to show what came after it.
The answer is False, friends. The second son said, “I will, sir…” but the text goes on, “But he did not go.” A nice yes with no vineyard behind it. That's the sting in the story.

The answer is the first son, friends. Jesus asks, “Which of the two did the will of his father?” and the chief priests and elders answer, “The first.” He's the one who said no and then went. What he did counted more than what he said.

The word is before, friends. Jesus says, “Truly I tell you, the tax collectors and prostitutes are entering the kingdom of God before you.” That's a sharp thing to say to the chief priests and elders. The tax collectors and prostitutes are going in ahead of them.

The answer is True, friends. Jesus tells the leaders, “…John came to you in the way of righteousness, and you did not believe him, but the tax collectors and prostitutes did.” They believed John, and the leaders did not. It matches the first son who ended up going.

The answer is False, friends. Jesus says, “And even after you saw this, you did not repent and believe him.” They saw the tax collectors and prostitutes believe John, and they still didn't repent. That's the second son's story all over again.
